title: Module 10 intro — Human-AI Interaction and Oversight

lines: Welcome to Module Ten: Human-AI Interaction and Oversight.
A human in charge sounds safe, but only if that human can actually catch mistakes.
Picture a fintech whose refunds agent handles thousands of requests a day.
To be safe, the team rules that every action needs a human click.
Each reviewer now faces four hundred approvals a day.
Most are small, routine refunds, and the agent is almost always right.
So the reviewers stop reading and start rubber-stamping.
The approval rate climbs to ninety-nine point eight percent.
Then comes a large refund to a brand-new account.
The agent is unsure, but its summary sounds completely confident.
The approve button is pre-selected, and the reviewer clicks in two seconds.
The money is gone, and the refund can't be reversed.
They had oversight on paper, but none in practice.
That's automation bias: over-trusting automated output and no longer checking it.
So they redesign around two questions: can it be undone, and how bad is a mistake?
Small refunds now run on their own, with monitoring and sampled audits.
Only large, irreversible refunds wait for human approval.
Clear triggers escalate the rest: low confidence, a value limit, or a customer asking for a person.
The review screen shows the evidence, and low-confidence cases look different.
Nothing is pre-selected, and a sample of approvals gets audited.
That's lesson one: three oversight models.
In the loop, a human approves first; on the loop, a human watches and can reverse; in command, humans set the limits.
You'll build approval interrupts that pause, save state, and resume.
And you'll hand off full context, so customers never repeat themselves.
Lesson two covers communicating uncertainty.
Raw model probabilities aren't reliable, so use simple confidence bands, and let the system say it doesn't know.
You'll also cover disclosing the AI, citing sources, and offering a route to a human.
Plus specific feedback, because human corrections are your best training data.
This domain is five percent of the exam, and it rewards one instinct: match oversight to reversibility and risk.
Approving everything is a wrong answer, and that's where lesson one begins.
